en: Now, the characteristics of the hand symbols, such as the vajra and the bell, are described.
Now, the characteristics of the hand symbols, such as the vajra and the bell, shall be explained.

A field measuring one *tāla* in length and breadth is divided into twelve parts. With a length three times that [width], by drawing lines through one and a half squares at the four corners in the eastern and western sections, and by omitting two squares each on the left and right of the center of the Brahma-line, a central pin (*madhyaśūcī*) is formed by laying down four lines from the middle of the eastern and western squares to the end of the Brahma-line.

The height and width of one *mtho* consists of two *cha chung*; its height is three times that [width]. By means of the preceding and succeeding parts, one draws half-squares around the four corners. Then, having set aside the two squares to the left and right of the center of the Brahma-line (*tshaṅs pa’i thig*), one strikes four lines at the ends of the Brahma-lines at the centers of the preceding and succeeding squares; these constitute the central points.
By removing two parts from each of the two sides of the double-pronged [vajra], there is a four-pronged one by means of those two parts on each side;
that is, by removing two parts from both faces of the two tips, there are four tips by means of those two parts each.
Its height is two parts,
emerging from the mouth of a makara.
It is beautified by two nostrils at its base,
which are like the snouts of lions.
Its shape is like a half-moon,
with its height being two parts [of the side] and its width being one-fourth part [of that].
With a height of eight parts, beautifully bent in three curves,
and resplendent with three streaks of light rays.
It is beautifully adorned by the three radiating rays of light.
In the central portion, however, by casting two lines each toward the four directions from the center of the Brahma-line and rotating [the cord] into a circle,
the *varaṭaka* (pericarp) is formed.
Above that, having set aside half a part for the girdle,
one should fashion a fully blossomed lotus with two parts.
Below and above the strands of the girdle, two fine strands should be attached to it.
One should act so that two fine strands are joined above and below the loops of the girdle.
A jewel garland should be made for the girdle.
In the waistband, a string of jewels should be fashioned.
Its filaments are made with half that portion.

Having produced the moon by means of one part— [this being] the completion of the moon by a single sixteenth [digit] through the elision of the remainder— it becomes the Samaya-vajra of the Blessed One.
When the remainder has been wiped away, it becomes the Vajra of the Blessed One’s Samaya.
The vajra should be made starting from four finger-breadths up to twenty finger-breadths;
for according to the scripture, one should not have it made beyond twenty [finger-breadths].
"One should not [perform it] twenty times or more," according to the scriptural authority (āgama).
In the corners of the wrathful deities, however, Karāla is formed by the removal of one part.
As for the wrathful [deities], their mouths are split open after removing one part from each corner.
By removing two spikes, it becomes three-spiked; by removing four spikes, it becomes single-spiked, which causes the paralysis of serpents.
By discarding both tips, it becomes single-pointed; this is the "serpent that stirs from all sides."
However, by making four spikes at the corners, it becomes nine-spoked; nevertheless, its central spike is circular.
The twenty-ninth [type] has four points at its corners; however, the central point is circular.
The universal vajra (viśvavajra), however, has twelve prongs, because three-pronged points are made on the four sides of the hub.
The twelve-pronged viśvavajra has three prongs made on each of the four sides of the hub.
That very [vajra], by means of making five prongs, becomes a twenty-pronged universal vajra.
By making that very [vajra] five-pointed, it becomes the twenty-pointed viśvavajra.
Furthermore, by adding five spikes each below and above that very [vajra], there is the Viśvavajra with thirty spikes. || 0 ||
Furthermore, it is said that by adding five points above and five below that very [vajra], there is the variegated vajra (*viśvavajra*) with thirty points.
The front portion of the bell is as before;
from the middle portion, half a part [is the size] of the moon.
The moon is formed by half of the central portion.
The filaments are half a part.
With one part, a lotus.
With one [part], a lotus.
The face of wisdom is one-fourth [of the total].
The vase is one-fourth [of that]. *Caturbhāgena kalaśam*. The fourth part is the vase.
The pedestal for the vase is made with two parts.
By removing four parts from each of the corners of the other [square], one creates an eight-petaled lotus,
complete with a pericarp and filaments.
Above the pericarp and below the pedestal,
one should fashion three lines in the form of a neck.
In the middle of two mekhala-s (girdles) made from half a part,
there is one part adorned with a garland of vajras.
In the center,
there are four parts where the necklaces and half-necklaces are situated.
As before, one part is adorned with a lower row of vajras.
On all sides, one part of the rim was cut away for the Great Vajradhara.
This is one part of the rim of universal certainty; it belongs to the Great Vajradhara.
But for Akṣobhya,
it is slightly open.

The center is adorned with necklaces (*hāra*) and half-necklaces (*ardhahāra*); within the necklaces, in the cardinal directions, are the wheel, the jewel, the lotus, and the double-vajra (*viśvavajra*)—or, in the place of the double-vajra, a sword—for Vairocana and the others.

In the center, adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, within the necklaces, in the directions, are the wheel, the jewel, the lotus, and the double-vajra; or else, in the place of the double-vajra, there is a sword, for Vairocana and the rest.
In the intermediate directions are the lotuses with vajra-stalks and vajra-seats,
and the blue lotuses (*utpala*) of Locanā and the other goddesses.

In place of the two rows of vajras above and below, there are rows of wheels (*cakra*), jewels (*ratna*), lotuses (*padma*), and double-vajras (*viśvavajra*); this is to be understood according to the divisions of the Tathāgata families. That is to say, in the places of Vairocana and the others, there is the symbol (*cihna*) of Akṣobhya.
The characteristics of Akṣobhya and the others are present in the abodes of Vairocana and the rest.
Here, the bell, starting from its neck, is made of pure bronze;
here, the bell, beginning from its neck, is of the nature of pure metal.
Above that, there are two parts consisting of gold and other materials, as well as a vajra.
Above that, two parts are also vajras composed of gold and other such substances.
The distinction is as follows: one bell has a face like a slightly blossoming lotus; another is cow-faced; and another is shaped like a lotus. ||o||
Some bells have slightly opened lotuses; some are like the faces of oxen; and some are in the form of lotuses—these are the distinctions.
Here, one should meditate upon Akṣobhya, Vairocana, and the others on the middle and the eastern and other spokes of the vajra, extending as far as the central hub (varaṭaka).
Here, one should visualize Akṣobhya, Vairocana, and the others at the center of the vajra and at the tips and the base of the eastern and other [spokes].

Alternatively, Vairocana is in the center, and in the petals starting from the east are Maitreya, Kṣitigarbha, Vajrapāṇi, Gaganagañja, Lokeśvara, Mañjuśrī, Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, and Samantabhadra; in the eight corners is Vajrasattva.

Alternatively, Vairocana is in the center, and on the petals in the east and so forth are Maitreya, Kṣitigarbha, Vajrapāṇi, Gaganagañja, Lokeśvara, Mañjuśrī, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Samantabhadra, and on the eighth position, Vajrasattva.
On the petals of the other lotus, starting from the east, are Vajrāṅkuśī, Vajrapāśī, Vajrasphoṭā, and Vajrāveśā;
in the southeast and the other directions are Cundrā,
Ratnolkā, Vajraśṛṅkhalā, and Aparājitā.
In the directions of the east and so forth, there are Cundā, Ratnajvālā, Vajraśṛṅkhalā, and Aparājitā.
In the center of the western prongs is Jñānaḍākinī; in the east, Vajraḍākinī; in the north, Ghorāḍākinī; in the west, Vettālī;
and in the south, Caṇḍālī. On the other prongs, in the center is Jñānaḍākinī; in the east, Vajraḍākinī; in the north, Vajraghorāḍākinī; in the west, Vetālī; and in the south, Caṇḍālī.

Upon the bell, on the downward-facing lotus petals in the cardinal directions, arranged clockwise, are Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārā; in the intermediate directions are Vasudhārā, Cundā, Bhṛkuṭī, and Vajramālā.

On the bell, on the downward-facing lotus petals in the cardinal directions, arranged clockwise, are Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārā; in the intermediate directions are Vasudhārā, Cundā, Bhṛkuṭī, and Vajramālā.
The face atop the jar is the body of Prajñāpāramitā.
Above that, there is a lotus, a moon, and a vajra,
as before.
The color and other attributes of these deities, such as Akṣobhya and the rest,
have been explained previously.

Then, having generated the deity as the *samayasattva*, one should summon the *jñānasattva* by means of light rays from the seed-syllable in the heart; having caused it to enter there preceded by the offering of water for honor (*argha*) and so forth, and having installed it according to the ritual rules, one performs the worship and other rites. Then, transforming the deities, they abide in the form of needles and so forth.

Then, having generated the deities of the commitment-being (samayasattva), one invites the wisdom-being (jñānasattva) with light rays from the seed-syllable at the heart. Preceded by the offering of water for the feet and so forth, one causes them to enter [the commitment-beings] and performs the consecration according to the ritual procedure. Having performed the offerings and so on, through the complete transformation of the deities, they are established in the form of the tips [of the vajra] and so forth.

Having developed firm conviction that the vajra is skillful means (*upāya*) and the bell is the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), and that both have the ultimate bodhicitta as their intrinsic nature, one should recite: *oṃ sarvatathāgatasiddhivajra samaye tiṣṭha eṣa tvāṃ dhārayāmi hīḥ hi hi hi hi hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā*. While reciting this, one should hold the vajra with the right thumb and ring finger; then, while reciting *oṃ vajraghaṇṭa hūṃ*, one should hold the bell with the left [thumb and ring finger], place it upon the left hip, and [visualize] Vajrasattva and the others.

With the resolve, "I shall delight [the assembly]," preceded by the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*, one should brandish the vajra while reciting: "O Vajra, lift it up! Deliver the beings through the seven liberations and the Dharma-liberations! O Vajra, strike! O Vajra, impel! Holding fast, *hūṃ* 2 *ho* 2! Thus one should brandish the vajra.

Having formed a firm conviction that the vajra is the nature of method and the bell is the essence of wisdom, and that both are ultimately the nature of bodhicitta, [recite]: oṃ sarvatathāgatasiddhivajrasamayastiṣṭha āḥ śāstvadharāya mi hīḥ hi hi hi hi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.

Having spoken thus, with the right hand [the fingers] from the thumb to the ring finger, and while reciting *oṃ vajraghaṇṭe hūṃ*, one should take hold of the bell with the left hand and rest it against the left shoulder; then, with the conviction that one is pleasing Vajrasattva and the others, one should proceed.
Reciting "so hi ai badzra mull'a lu t'a ri ātva bi mokkha dha ram bi mo kbeM b'a dzdzdza tu hūṃ b'adzdzdza tu hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hoḥ," one should brandish the vajra.

Placing that vajra on the right hip or brandishing it, one should first recite: *oṃ vajradharma raṇita praraṇita saṃpraraṇita sarvabuddhakṣetrapracāline prajñāpāramitānādasvabhāve vajrasattvahṛdayasaṃtoṣaṇi hūṃ 2 ho 2 svāhā*, while moving the bell and the staff-like arm.

Then, resting the vajra on the right shoulder or brandishing it, one recites: *oṃ vajradharmaratnita praraṇita saṃpraraṇita sarvabuddhakṣetrapraticchali te prajñāpāramitānādasambhave vajrasattva hṛdaya saṃtoṣaṇi hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ ho ho hoḥ svāhā*. Having spoken thus, by moving the staff-like arm, one strikes the first bell.
One should ring the bell at the navel, then at the heart, the throat, the mouth, the two nostrils,
the two ears, the two eyes, and finally on the head.
From the navel and the heart, then to the throat, the two apertures of the mouth and nose, the two eyes, and those four [together] at the crown of the head—one should ring the bell. Thus it is said.

Preceded by the brandishing of the vajra and bell, one should ring the bell while reciting the mantra as taught in the tantra. One should perform the *kamalāvarta* three or five times between the knees. Thus concludes the procedure for the characteristics and so forth of the vajra and bell.
Thus concludes the ritual concerning the characteristics of the vajra and the vajra bell, and so forth.
